https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: It wasn't the story Rabbi Shlomo Bochner went looking for. It was the story that found him. During a visit to Prague, an encounter with renowned historian Yehuda Geberer opened the door to a tale long forgotten, as one conversation led to another, and one question uncovered the next. Before long, they were following the trail of a story that began decades ago - one whose echoes reach far closer to home than anyone could have imagined. Join Rabbi Shlomo Bochner on an unforgettable journey in Echoes from the Platform , streaming this Tisha B'Av.

Picture: YURIY DYACHYSHYN / AFP via Getty Images Thu, 30 Jul, 2026 - 15:58 Peter Beaumont and agencies       Russia has been accused of violating Polish airspace, after a missile exploded in a field in the east of the country, triggering Nato air defences, in the midst of a massive air raid that killed 13 people in neighbouring Ukraine . Polish authorities said that the explosion near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia, close to Lublin, had created a 10-metre-wide crater. Residents of Tarnawa-Kolonia reported hearing an explosion at about 4am that shook the windows of their homes, police said. Nato’s supreme ⁠allied commander for Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, said: “​Nato ​will continue ​to take all necessary ​measures ‌to defend Nato ​territory.” Speaking at the scene of the explosion, in a field about 50 miles from the Ukrainian border, the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said the missile was most likely Russian. “From the analysis of most of the traces, the recovered fragments point to a Russian KH-101 missile,” he told journalists. Read More Thousands of French wildfire evacuees return home as cooler weather moves in US man hikes out of mountains to get help after he was impaled by trekking pole Time running out for survivors after quake in south-west Japan He said there was no reason to think that Poland had been the target of the missile but said the Polish military had been prepared to shoot it down if it threatened a built-up area. As the attacks on Ukraine took place, Poland – a Nato member – scrambled fighter jets to protect its airspace, its armed forces said. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said in a post on X that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had crossed into Poland. The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. People hide in a Kyiv metro station, during an air raid. Picture: Credit Dmytro Laryn / Ukrainska Pravda António Costa, the president of the EU council, said on X: “Last night, Russia launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine. During the attack, Polish airspace was also violated, underlining once again that Russia’s aggression is a threat to the security of Europe as a whole.” Ursula von der ​Leyen, the European Commission president, said the ⁠Russian missile incident ⁠in ⁠Poland was ​another “unacceptable violation” of the ⁠EU’s airspace. At least 13 people in Ukraine – including one in Kyiv – died in Thursday’s attacks, which extended as far ⁠as the western city of Lviv. A missile strike in the central city of Kryvyi Rih – Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s home town – killed at least six people, including two girls, aged five and 12, the head of the town’s military administration said. Zelenskyy had warned the country hours in advance of Moscow launching the massive attack. Oleksandr Vilkul, the ‌head of the defence council, said: “In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults.” Eight more people were wounded, he said. Another six people, including two children, were killed in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava. The military administration for Kyiv confirmed one death, with the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reporting fires in several districts. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!” A Ukrainian soldier, at the bomb damaged Lukianivska district of Kyiv, Ukraine, looks up at the damaged buildings. Picture: Niall Carson/PA Wire In ‌Lviv, close to Poland, rescue workers were scrambling to clear rubble to reach those trapped after Russian missiles damaged two blocks of flats and injured 26 people, officials said. Late on Wednesday, Zelenskyy had posted: “The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight … Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe.” Zelenskyy also repeated his request to Ukraine’s allies to supply Kyiv with the missiles its air defence system lacked. “It is important that our partners fully ​understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles.” A residential apartment building is seen damaged after a Russian strike on Kyiv, Ukraine, Thursday, July 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky) Russia’s defence ministry, commenting on the strikes, said it had used land, sea and air-launched missiles, as well as strike drones, during the raid and claimed it had targeted military industrial facilities. Elsewhere on Thursday, the ⁠Ukrainian military struck four Russian ⁠tankers ​in the Black Sea ⁠and the Sea of ⁠Azov, Ukraine’s drone ​forces ‌commander, ‌Robert Brovdi, said. Brovdi said on the Telegram app that 205 tankers – ​130 in the Sea of Azov ⁠and 75 ​in the ​Black ​Sea –had ​been ‌hit in the ​past ​three weeks. - The Guardian Read More Iranian missile hits Chinese firm’s building in Kuwait amid renewed strikes x Every Match. https://www.deccanchronicle.com/opinion/.text: On August 7, 2026, a trilateral mutual defence agreement was signed between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in Mecca. The venue, which has Islam’s holiest mosque, symbolises a convergence of three powerful Islamic nations. The mutual defence clause reflects Article 5 of the Nato agreement. Though Egypt had joined the negotiations earlier, it kept away. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidann, expects it to join soon. Turkish leaders emphasised that the agreement was not aimed at any country and was a purely defensive measure. Though not a “Middle Eastern Nato”, some term it the “Islamic Nato”. Members of Nato had shared concerns about countering the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact countries. In fact, their joining the 2001 US intervention in Afghanistan went beyond the original mandate. Also, Nato countries have a joint command and control syatem and a shared nuclear deterrence, though the US retains the control of forward-deployed nuclear weapons. The three Mecca agreement nations have some, not totally, overlapping threat concerns. Turkey has had differences with Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu even declared that “our next target is Turkey”. Consequently, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced that “now you can’t even touch our hair”. Turkey has berated Israeli military intrusions into Lebanon and pressure on the Syrian regime, which Turkey helped install. Turkey’s relations with Iran have fluctuated. But they share an interest in containing the aspirations of the Kurdish community which dominates eastern Turkey, the northern parts of Syria and Iraq as well as western Iran. Reportedly, Turkey restrained Israel from employing Iraqi Kurds for a ground operation against Iran, co-opting Iran’s Kurdish minority, at the start of the US-Israeli war. Ironically, the Turkish Ottoman Empire, after recapturing Diriyah, the first Saudi state, in 1818, took the al-Saud family ruler and his sons prisoner. They were beheaded in Istanbul, then Constantinople, in 1818. Recent Saudi-Turkish differences first arose over Turkey supporting the Arab Spring in 2010-11. Then came the brutal killing of American journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. Now the shared threats eclipse the past differences. Saudi Arabia basically perceives a threat from Iran and its allies like Yemen’s Houthis and Iraq’s pro-Iran militias. Yemen has had a truce since 2022, but recently the Houthis targeted Saudi Arabia’s Aramco oil facility. Regarding Israel, the Saudis have resisted US pressure to sign the 2020 Abraham Accords and normalise relations, demanding that Israel must first present a pathway to a Palestinian state. In fact, the Saudis hurriedly signed a mutual defence agreement with Pakistan in September 2025, days after Israel targeted Hamas in Qatar, which created a perception of the US being unable or unwilling to control Israel targeting the GCC countries. However, the US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28 triggered the Iranian retaliation on US military bases and assets in the GCC nations. Thus, the present Mecca agreement covers Saudi Arabia’s perceived threats from both Israel and Iran plus its allies. Pakistan presents a different case. Since independence, it has repeatedly tried grabbing the India-controlled Jammu and Kashmir by force or multilateral UN intervention or terrorism-based blackmail. After 1947, while India chose nonalignment during the Cold War, Pakistan accepted military alliances with the US and Britain. In 1954, it signed the mutual defence assistance agreement with the US for obtaining military assistance in exchange for an anti-Communist posture. The new Air Force aircraft and the Army’s tanks gave Pakistan a military advantage over India, which instead was focused on development and not strengthening its defence forces. China militarily defeating India in 1962 and the 1964 death of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru left the Indian defence forces demoralised and under-equipped. Perceiving Indian vulnerability, Pakistan tried in 1965 to militarily grab Kashmir, but failed. The military alliance with the United States slowly weakened after Pakistan declined to send troops to assist America during the Vietnam War. It eventually collapsed after India won the 1971 war, leading to the creation of Bangladesh. Pakistan since then has aligned with China as both countries want to contain India while keeping their outstanding disputes alive. In between, Pakistan again became the military spearhead of the US-Saudi countering of the Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan in 1979. In the new trilateral arrangement, the Saudis bring oil wealth and religious standing; Turks contribute a modern army and weapons compliant with Nato standards; and Pakistan represents the only Islamic nation possessing nuclear weapons. Photograph: GoFundMe US crime Four victims identified in Louisiana stabbing spree after suspect detained Woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend identified as victims in incident that also critically wounded a child Ramon Antonio Vargas Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.13 EDT First published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Louisiana woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend have been identified as the four victims killed in a stabbing spree on Saturday that also left a young child critically wounded in the southern part of the state, according to a relative and family advocate. Verna Mae Verdin, her daughter Letha Verrett, her son Paul Verret, and his girlfriend Krissy Lynn Parfait were stabbed to death at their home in the community of Houma, the relative and advocate, Brandon Thiel, told Louisiana television news station WVUE and said on an online campaign raising funds in part for the victims’ funeral expenses. The wounded child reportedly was Verdin’s six-year-old grandson, who happened to be spending Saturday night with her. Local authorities have not formally identified any of the victims of Saturday’s stabbing spree but did say they had detained a 47-year-old man named Kaegan Jude Solet in connection with the case. Thiel told WVUE that Solet had fathered a child with one of the slain victims. It is not the first time Solet has been accused of violent behavior. He had previously been tried but acquitted of attempted murder in the December 2019 stabbing of a woman inside a Houma hotel, WVUE reported, citing criminal court documents. Solet had also been booked in the January 2019 stabbing death of an unhoused man named Scott Lovell, according to reporting from the news website HoumaToday.com. Lovell’s mother, Nancy Guidry, told WVUE on Sunday that a grand jury subsequently failed to indict Solet. The bloodshed in Houma on Saturday came about two years after Louisiana’s department of health warned that intimate partner violence was a “significant public health concern in the state”. The state’s rate of women murdered by men has historically been significantly higher than the national average, according to the Louisiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence . Meanwhile, across the US, more than half of female homicide victims are killed by current or former male intimate partners, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) crime data show. Verdin was planning to retire in two weeks from a 20-year career at Walmart at the time of Saturday’s killings, as Thiel put it to WVUE. Thiel said Letha Verret was a mother herself and had seven children, including three who are minors. Paul Verrett and Krissy Lynn Parfait lived together in a camper behind Letha and Verdin, WVUE reported. Investigators said on Sunday that deputies with the Terrebonne parish sheriff’s office, which patrols Houma, initially encountered the wounded child while responding to reports of a “series of stabbing incidents”. Deputies reported that they then found Verdin, the Verret siblings and Parfait dead nearby. A WVUE journalist on Sunday reported being told by the sheriff’s office that the wounded boy had run to a neighbor who called for emergency help in the aftermath of the mass murder. Thiel told WVUE that the boy is a “full of energy, smiling child that [is] just the light of so many of the family’s world”. “Thankfully, he was able to make it out,” Thiel remarked. He also said, “They are processing a lot right now. They are trying to process the loss of family members.” Community members rallied around Verdin’s family as news of the killings spread around Houma and beyond. The fundraising campaign Thiel had organized to support covering the slain’s victims’ funeral expenses and medical costs for the wounded boy had exceeded $46,500 by Monday morning. As of Monday, there had been at least 19 mass murders in the US for the year so far, according to statistics tracked by the Guardian. Two of those mass murders had been reported in Louisiana, including a case in April in which eight children were shot to death in the city of Shreveport in what the police described as a “violent domestic incident”. A mass murder is defined as a case in which four or more victims are killed. In the US, most such cases are carried out by attackers with guns. Texas authorities reported a mass murder on Sunday near the community of San Benito. Investigators there said they could not immediately release many details – but they confirmed four adults who were related had been shot to death, and one suspect had been taken into custody, the Texas television news outlet KVEO reported. https://www.politico.eu/article/zelensky.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has a right to be angry. In a wretched month for Ukrainians, ahead of a fast-approaching frigid winter, Donald Trump’s “very big and important deal” to acquire millions of tons of diesel fuel from Russia couldn’t have come at a worse time. The U.S. president’s plan to lift sanctions on Moscow to allow diesel imports came as a sucker punch for most Ukrainians enduring barrages of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, with civilian casualties mounting. Advertisement Advertisement The question for Zelenskyy is just how angry he can actually afford to be. “His showing his frustration is understandable, but there are downsides,” said Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat and fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. The Ukrainian president immediately dubbed Trump’s deal a “weak decision” and “a gift to Putin” that will fund Russia’s war. Even more defiantly, he approved further drone strikes on Russian refineries, prompting Trump to call for Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader. Zelenskyy shows no signs of heeding Trump’s command to “better damn well stop” striking at Russia’s energy industry. That’s very much a continuation of his loss of patience this year, which has seen him sharpening his rhetoric toward both critics and allies, rebuking European leaders for moving too slowly with support, trading barbs with Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, and openly questioning Trump’s approach to the war. The tougher tone reflects mounting exasperation in Kyiv — especially with the U.S. president. Ukraine’s defense resilience and innovations with drones and missiles have augmented Zelenskyy’s confidence and readiness to push back. And yet, venting his frustration is not without risks. Willasey-Wilsey suspects Zelenskyy may be calculating that Trump could emerge weakened from next month’s midterms, especially as some Republicans are already breaking ranks over the diesel deal. But the Ukrainian leader risks provoking Trump into cutting off vital U.S. intelligence support or pressuring Elon Musk to disable SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, on which Ukraine’s military heavily relies. Advertisement Advertisement Zelenskyy may be underestimating “how dangerous a wounded Trump could be” for Ukraine, warned Willasey-Wilsey. The Trump administration has also threatened to halt a program through which allies purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine, the Financial Times reported Monday. That would cause a major upheaval in supplies and force Kyiv to rely even more on its European allies, who are already struggling to rearm. But Zelenskyy is standing firm. He insists Ukraine will only halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its air barrage. “Any de-escalation steps must be mutual,” he wrote on Telegram. He has backing from an unlikely quarter: opposition lawmakers who are usually fierce critics of his leadership. Even former President Petro Poroshenko, a bitter political rival, defended Zelenskyy against Trump’s call for his replacement. “If anyone needs a new leader, it is Russia,” Poroshenko said in comments. “For me, the key question is simple: Are we any closer to a full and unconditional ceasefire? That is the only lens through which any move should be assessed.” Advertisement Advertisement Trump’s calls to replace Zelenskyy ironically strengthen the Ukrainian leader’s position at home, opposition lawmaker Mykola Knyazhitskiy said. “There’s no greater campaigner for Zelenskyy than Donald Trump,” he added. “After every such conflict, Zelenskyy’s approval rating rises both in Ukraine and among our allies, particularly in Europe.” But Trump’s ability to force Kyiv into a settlement has diminished, according to Nathalie Tocci, who advised two former EU foreign policy chiefs. Having already withdrawn most American support, Trump has reduced his leverage over Ukraine and Europe, she argues. He could still inflict considerable damage by suspending intelligence sharing, but she doubts he would do so indefinitely or halt weapons sales. “If money is involved, I can’t see him pulling the plug on sales,” she said. But the fear in Kyiv is that Trump’s pursuit of a deal with Moscow will come at Ukraine’s expense. Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a prominent opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister, sees little prospect of Putin compromising. “He’s not ready to stop the war or even agree a ceasefire,” she said. “From my understanding, all the other ‘deals’ which have supposedly been discussed by U.S. negotiators with the Russians have been only about the capitulation of Ukraine and basically the country ceasing to exist as a free, independent, sovereign state.” That likely explains Zelenskyy’s open anger. He knows that antagonizing Trump comes at a price. But so does appeasing a U.S. president who seems increasingly willing to do business with Putin. For Ukraine, neither option is good. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/16/at-l.text: At least 12 people died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Gambia, the Red Cross said.The incident occurred off of Jinack Kajata in the country's North Bank region, the Gambia Red Cross Society (GRCS) said on Thursday. The migrants were reportedly heading towards Europe via the West African Atlantic Route."The number of people missing remains uncertain, and further updates are expected as response efforts continue," the GRCS said in a statement, adding that it was "working closely with relevant authorities and response partners as the situation unfolds."According to Gambian media, the village of Jinack Kajata on Jinack Island has become an increasingly popular launch site for migrants looking to make the journey to Spain's Canary Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.The United Nations' International Organization for Migration (IOM) says the West African Atlantic Route is a key pathway for West African migrants travelling to Europe, despite it becoming increasingly dangerous."Data from the West African Atlantic Route show that while arrivals to the Canary Islands fell considerably since the 2024 peak (62 per cent decrease from 2024 to 2025), recorded deaths and disappearances remained broadly unchanged, falling 4 per cent from 2024 to 2025 (1,215 to 1,172), highlighting how the route has become much more dangerous for migrants," the IOM said earlier this week.It added that increased controls in traditional departure spots in Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal have pushed some migrants seeking to reach Europe further south, towards countries such as The Gambia."These alternative departure points can add up to 750 kilometres to the crossing, extending some journeys to approximately 2,200 kilometres and exposing people to longer periods at sea, more remote and less monitored coastlines, and greater risks of shipwreck, dehydration and disappearance," the IOM said.In July, dozens of migrants were reportedly dead or missing after a vessel travelling from The Gambia was shipwrecked off the coast of Mauritania.

CCIB Recognizes the Business Performance of Companies in Districts 1 and 6 of Bucharest Business & Investments Economics News Published on October 16, 2026 By Magda Purice Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email The Bucharest Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCIB) recognized the economic achievements of companies operating in Districts 1 and 6 of Bucharest on Wednesday, the 14 th of October, as part of the Bucharest Company Rankings – District Stage. The event took place in the “Carol I” Auditorium of the CCIB Palace.â “The achievements we are celebrating today are the result of your hard work, courage, and sense of responsibility. Behind every award-winning company are important decisions, investments, sustained efforts, and teams of people who contribute every day to the success of the businesses they represent. That is why I believe this ceremony is, first and foremost, an opportunity to thank you for believing in your own projects, for your perseverance in overcoming challenges, and for the essential role you play in the economic and social development of Bucharest,” said CCIB President Iuliu Stocklosa in his opening remarks. The ceremony recognized the achievements of 4,096 companies in District 1, which recorded a combined turnover of more than 345 billion LEI in 2025 and an operating profit of 33.15 billion LEI. The activities of these companies also supported more than 222,000 jobs. “I believe that one of the most important changes public administration needs to make is to become genuinely transparent or, rather, to build a culture of true transparency. Not merely transparent communication, open dialogue, and project proposals, but real transparency rooted in an organizational culture. Transparency as a way of working, with decisions clearly explained and public funds monitored with clarity and accountability. I believe transparency is the antidote to corruption, pointless bureaucracy, and wasted effort,” said Iulian Hatmanu, Deputy Mayor of District 1. The achievements of 3,134 companies in District 6 of Bucharest were also highlighted. In 2025, these companies recorded a combined turnover of 99 billion LEI. Their operating profit amounted to 7.63 billion LEI, while the number of jobs they generated exceeded 113,000. “I believe that developing the community as a whole requires a partnership between public authorities and the business community. Public authorities have an obligation and a responsibility to create a predictable environment for businesses, put forward concrete proposals, and provide incentives so that, together, we can develop the community. Nothing can be achieved without the private sector,” said Ionuț Alexe, Director General of the Directorate General for Digitalization and European Funding within the District 6 City Hall. The award ceremony was attended by entrepreneurs from Districts 1 and 6 of Bucharest, representatives of local public administrations, as well as officials from the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Bucharest Chamber of Commerce and Industry will continue its series of events celebrating business performance with the Company Rankings for Districts 2 and 5, scheduled for the 21 st of October, followed by the Bucharest Company Rankings ceremony, which will take place on the 28 th of October.
